source_refs.note: Exercise 9.2, Question 16 (book page 273); the book prints no answers for Exercise 9.2; answers checked with sympy and the solution book

blocks.explanation:
The left side has the shape \(2\tan^{-1} t\) from Question 14 (i).
Plan: put \(t = \tan\frac{\theta}{2}\tan\frac{\phi}{2}\), use \(2\tan^{-1} t = \cos^{-1}\frac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}\), and show with half-angle formulas that \(\frac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2} = \frac{\cos\theta + \cos\phi}{1 + \cos\theta\cos\phi}\).
steps:
Given: \(t = \tan\frac{\theta}{2}\tan\frac{\phi}{2}\).
To prove: \(2\tan^{-1} t = \cos^{-1}\frac{\cos\theta + \cos\phi}{1 + \cos\theta\cos\phi}\).
Method: Question 14 (i) changes \(2\tan^{-1} t\) into \(\cos^{-1}\frac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}\). Then only algebra is left: write \(t^2\) with \(\tan^2\frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos\theta}{1 + \cos\theta}\), which brings in \(\cos\theta\) and \(\cos\phi\).

Use Question 14 (i)
\[2\tan^{-1} t = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}\quad (1)\]
Why: Question 14 (i) with \(x = t\); it needs \(t \ge 0\) (see the last steps).

Write \(t^2\) (put \(a = \cos\theta\), \(b = \cos\phi\))
\[t^2 = \dfrac{(1 - a)(1 - b)}{(1 + a)(1 + b)}\]
Why: Multiply the half-angle results for \(\theta\) and \(\phi\). Short letters keep the algebra readable.

Clear the inner fractions
\[\dfrac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2} = \dfrac{(1+a)(1+b) - (1-a)(1-b)}{(1+a)(1+b) + (1-a)(1-b)}\]
Why: Multiply top and bottom by \((1 + a)(1 + b)\).

Expand
\[(1+a)(1+b) = 1 + a + b + ab\]
\[(1-a)(1-b) = 1 - a - b + ab\]
\[\text{top} = 2a + 2b\]
\[\text{bottom} = 2 + 2ab\]
Why: Subtracting cancels \(1\) and \(ab\); adding cancels \(a\) and \(b\).

Simplify
\[\dfrac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2} = \dfrac{2(a + b)}{2(1 + ab)}\]
\[= \dfrac{\cos\theta + \cos\phi}{1 + \cos\theta\cos\phi}\]
Why: Cancel the 2 and put back \(a = \cos\theta\), \(b = \cos\phi\).

Put into (1)
\[2\tan^{-1}\left(\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}\tan\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\]
\[= \cos^{-1}\dfrac{\cos\theta + \cos\phi}{1 + \cos\theta\cos\phi}\]
Why: The fraction inside \(\cos^{-1}\) in (1) is the one we just found.

Where the result holds
\[t = \tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}\tan\dfrac{\phi}{2} \ge 0\]
Why: Question 14 (i) needs \(t \ge 0\). This is true in the usual case \(0 \le \theta < \pi\), \(0 \le \phi < \pi\) (both half-angles in \(\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\)). If \(t < 0\), e.g. \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\phi = -\frac{\pi}{2}\), the left side is \(2\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{2}\) but the right side is \(\cos^{-1} 0 = \frac{\pi}{2}\).

Check
\[\theta = \phi = \dfrac{\pi}{3}:\ 2\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.6435\]
\[\cos^{-1}\dfrac{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}}{1 + \frac{1}{4}} = \cos^{-1}\tfrac{4}{5} \approx 0.6435\]
Why: \(\tan\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(t = \frac{1}{3}\); both sides agree.
